html:
In 1338 and 1339 a deadly disease struck a Christian trading community in the Chuy valley, near Lake Issyk-Kul in today's Kyrgyzstan. It is the earliest known outbreak of the plague that became the Black Death.

The community belonged to the Church of the East, Christians who lived along the Silk Road, then within the Chagatai Khanate. Russian archaeologists dug up their cemeteries in the 1880s. Many gravestones, written in Syriac, give the years 1338 and 1339, and some say the person died of "pestilence".

In 2022 scientists studied ancient DNA from teeth in these graves. They found Yersinia pestis, the plague bacterium. The strain sat at the very root of the family tree that led to the Black Death, and it was close to strains still found in wild marmots of the nearby Tian Shan mountains. This suggests the pandemic began in or near Central Asia.

From there the plague spread west along trade routes. By 1346 it had reached the Golden Horde on the Black Sea, and from there ships carried it to Europe, where it killed perhaps a third to a half of the people.
sum: In 1338 and 1339 a deadly disease struck a Christian trading community in the Chuy valley, near Lake Issyk-Kul in today's Kyrgyzstan. It is the earliest known outbreak of the plague that became the Black Death.
